# Graph `example_graph`

## Is it available here?

Run `graph graphs --json`. Use this skill only if an item named `example_graph` is listed (title: Example graph). Pass `--graph example_graph` to every command, as the examples here do, so they work in every directory; a project whose pointer makes `example_graph` the default may leave it out.

Before your first `graph` command, load the `graph-cli` skill as well: it explains the commands, the output envelope and safe writes. This skill says what the graph holds. Two of its ground rules apply from the first call:

- Run each call as a plain command that starts with `graph`: no `cd`, variables, loops, pipes or heredocs, which a restricted harness refuses. If a call is refused, run it again in that form before you give up.
- For a few fields, a count or a join, use `graph query` and `RETURN` only those columns (`graph describe schema --compact --json` lists the patterns), or `--fields <attr>,<attr>` on `find`, `get` and `neighbors`, instead of filtering JSON with another program.

## What is in it

| Module | Prefix | What it holds | Types | Links to other modules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `notes_and_sources` | `nas` | Notes about topics that cite their sources and assert claims. | 5 | `provenance` (1 out, 0 in) |

Built-in modules, shared by every graph: `core`, `provenance`.

- Before you work in a module, read it: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph --json` lists its types, its relations, its links to and from other modules (with the other module named) and its rules.
- To find a term whose module you do not know: `graph describe search <text> --graph example_graph --json` (types, relations, fields, enum values and states).
- For the fields, states and relations of one type: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.

| Type | What it is | Fields | States |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nas:Note` (`NOTE-0001`) | A short piece of writing about one or more topics. | `title` (required); `body` (required); `kind` (required, one of `observation`, `summary`, `question`) | `status`: `draft` <-> `published`, `draft` or `published` -> `archived`; initial `draft`; terminal `archived` |
| `nas:Topic` (`TOPIC-0001`) | A subject that notes are about. | `label` (required, unique); `synonyms` (many); `misspellings` (many); `description` | none |

Other types of the model, described in `references/model.md`: `nas:Book`, `nas:Source`, `nas:WebPage`, `provenance:Claim`.

Relations:

| Relation | From -> to | Cardinality | Notes | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nas:about` | `nas:Note` -> `nas:Topic` | out 1..n | inverse `has_note` | The note is about the topic. |
| `nas:asserts` | `nas:Note` -> `provenance:Claim` | out 0..n | inverse `asserted_in` | The note asserts the claim. |
| `nas:broader` | `nas:Topic` -> `nas:Topic` | out 0..n | acyclic, transitive, inverse `narrower` | The target topic is more general than the source topic. |
| `nas:cites` | `nas:Note` -> `nas:Source` | out 0..n | qualifiers `locator`, inverse `cited_by` | The note uses information from the source. |

As patterns for `graph query`:

```
(:Note)-[:about]->(:Topic)
(:Note)-[:asserts]->(:Claim)
(:Topic)-[:broader]->(:Topic)
(:Note)-[:cites]->(:Source)
```

Constraints:

- `nas:Note` `status` `draft` -> `published`: A note needs a body before it is published. (guard `nas.body_not_empty`)
- Rule `nas.summary_cites_source` on `nas:Note` (error, checked on every write): A published summary note cites at least one source.
- Rule `nas.topic_not_orphan` on `nas:Topic` (warning, checked in batch): A topic has notes or narrower topics.

## Names and ids

- Aliases: `nas:Note` `NOTE-0001`, `nas:Topic` `TOPIC-0001`. The number is zero-padded to 4 digits (`NOTE-0001`, never `NOTE-1`) and grows past 9999. A full id works everywhere; on the command line 8 or more trailing hex digits of it work too.
- `graph lookup <value> --graph example_graph --json` finds entities by name, ignoring case; it matches these fields, not other text:
  - `nas:Book`: `title` (main name)
  - `nas:Note`: `title` (main name)
  - `nas:Topic`: `label` (main name), `synonyms` (other names), `misspellings` (hidden names, matched but never shown)
  - `nas:WebPage`: `title` (main name)
- Names are not unique, so `lookup` returns candidates. Use the returned alias or id only when exactly one candidate matches exactly (`match.kind` is `exact`). With several candidates, or only prefix matches, do not answer about one of them first: list them with their names and ask which one is meant, then answer.
- `graph search <value> --graph example_graph --json` searches names and every text field, forgiving case, accents, typos and parts of words. Its results are suggestions: read one with `graph get` before you use it.
- Before you create an entity of one of these types, search for its name and its short forms. If one is the same thing, use it and add the new name to its other names field instead of creating another. When you create one, fill its other names fields with the abbreviations and synonyms people use. A write finding `data.semantic.possible_duplicate` names entities that already carry the name or a near spelling of it.

## Model

Every type with all its fields, lifecycles, relations and rules: [references/model.md](references/model.md). The live source, which wins when they differ: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
